chapter: The 1920s road: dance style and management
title: The only black act on the bill, next to closing
summary: They dressed upstairs, were treated no differently, and were always the only colored act on a bill, held in the next-to-closing spot.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Were you treated in any particular way because you were black?
No. Nope. Only thing about it, we had to dress upstairs instead

of dressing downstairs. All the dancers and colored fellows would have to dress upstairs. But they couldn't put us on No. 2 because nobody would follow us, so we went on next to closing. The act was so strong.
But you weren't treated in any particular way by managers of the theaters or the other white performers?
You were the only black act.
On tour, yeah, only black act, yep.
On this program or in general?
In general, always the only colored act on the program, in general. Never had two colored acts on the program.
Ain't necessary. There weren't any good colored acts on the road. What are you going to do with them? What are they going to do? Going to dance, too?
Perhaps there were different kinds of acts. There was more than one white act.
Yeah, because versatile, versatile. White acts were versatile acts. They had sketches to do, too. Tell me what you want to --
The black acts were more or less versatile?

Well, you see, in those days, they only get a dancer, a team dancer, negroes, a comedy dancing team. Understand? To hold down the No. 2 spot in the show, you know. That's what that was for, I'm sure. We didn't have to go through that no time at all. I don't think we ever went through that. But if we did, I don't remember. The act was

always up, had to be on next to closing. Always took that next to closing spot, recognized throughout the world of entertainment. So now we do two weeks up in Canada and coming out of there -- of course I got on the manager about the no billing situation, I talked to our la wyer about it and he said maybe there wasn't enough to do nothin'with, so I let that stall. Finally we went into "Blackbirds" in 1929. We traded vaudeville, pulled our circuit, all the different vaudeville circuits in the theaters during the time we left finally the "Blackbirds" came out in 1929, Lew Leslie's "Blackbirds."
